presentingComplaint: High fever with rigors for 8 days, now acutely unwell with breathlessness, confusion and near-collapse.
history: 48-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and neglected dental caries, referred from a district hospital after 8 days of intermittent high fever with rigors, drenching sweats, anorexia and progressive exertional breathlessness. Over the preceding 48 hours he developed increasing lethargy and reduced urine output, and on the morning of admission had a transient loss of consciousness. Family report painful red spots on his fingers and a small painless red patch on the sole. He had a dental extraction about 6 weeks earlier without antibiotic cover. No prior valve disease known, no prosthetic valve, no injection drug use. On arrival he is hypotensive and requires noradrenaline to maintain perfusion.
examination: Toxic, drowsy but rousable, warm peripheries with prolonged capillary refill. Splinter haemorrhages in two nail beds, tender violaceous nodules on the finger pulps (Osler nodes) and a non-tender erythematous macule on the right sole (Janeway lesion). New early-diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a wide pulse pressure. Bibasal crepitations. Mild splenic tenderness. Fundi show a Roth spot. No neck stiffness; no focal limb weakness but globally slowed.
imaging: Transthoracic echo suggests aortic valve vegetation with significant aortic regurgitation; transoesophageal echo confirms a 14 mm mobile vegetation on the non-coronary aortic cusp with a small root abscess and severe eccentric AR. Chest radiograph shows early pulmonary oedema. CT brain shows a small right parietal embolic infarct without haemorrhage.
microbiology: Three sets of blood cultures drawn from separate sites before antibiotics; two sets flag positive at 12 h and all sets by 24 h growing Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-sensitive (MSSA) — oxacillin S, cefazolin S, vancomycin S. Repeat cultures at 48 h remain positive (persistent bacteraemia) then clear by day 4 after source-directed therapy. Modified Duke criteria: 2 major (typical organism in persistently positive cultures; echocardiographic vegetation + new regurgitation) = definite IE.
differentialDiagnoses: Infective endocarditis (native aortic valve, MSSA) with septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction
Undifferentiated septic shock from another source
Primary Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia without endocarditis
Cardiac implantable device / catheter-related bloodstream infection
finalDiagnosis: Definite native-valve infective endocarditis (aortic valve, methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus) complicated by septic shock, acute kidney injury and a septic embolic cerebral infarct.
citations: American Heart Association — Infective Endocarditis in Adults: Diagnosis, Antimicrobial Therapy and Management of Complications — 2015
European Society of Cardiology — Guidelines for the Management of Endocarditis — 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Infective Endocarditis
stewardship: Sepsis-of-uncertain-source bundle applied within 1 hour: three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics, lactate, fluid resuscitation and early noradrenaline for shock. Because the patient is in septic shock with valvular findings and MRSA cannot be excluded empirically, start broad empiric IV vancomycin (loading then AUC-guided) to cover MRSA, with the option of adding an anti-staphylococcal/antipseudomonal beta-lactam per local acute-IE protocol. Once cultures confirm MSSA and susceptibility, de-escalate promptly to a narrow anti-staphylococcal agent — IV flucloxacillin (or cefazolin if penicillin intolerance) — and stop vancomycin; MSSA is more effectively cleared by beta-lactams than vancomycin. Adjunctive gentamicin is NOT recommended for native-valve staphylococcal IE (nephrotoxicity without benefit). Total duration ~6 weeks from first negative culture given the root abscess. Early Endocarditis-Team and cardiac-surgery referral for valve replacement is indicated for the perivalvular abscess, severe AR with heart failure and systemic embolisation. Daily blood cultures until clearance; monitor renal function and vancomycin levels while on empiric cover.
contraindications: Avoid aminoglycoside (gentamicin) in native-valve staphylococcal IE, especially with acute kidney injury
Avoid nephrotoxin stacking (NSAIDs, contrast without hydration) given AKI
Withhold anticoagulation for the embolic cerebral infarct in native-valve IE (haemorrhagic transformation risk)
Beta-lactam allergy must be verified before switching to flucloxacillin/cefazolin
edgeCases: Culture-negative endocarditis if antibiotics were given before cultures — would need serology for Coxiella/Bartonella and prolonged incubation
If isolate were MRSA, empiric vancomycin (or daptomycin) is continued rather than de-escalated to a beta-lactam
New heart block on ECG would signal extension of the root abscess and mandate urgent surgery
Persistent bacteraemia beyond 5-7 days despite appropriate therapy suggests uncontrolled focus / metastatic infection
expectedMaiK: In septic shock with a new regurgitant murmur, embolic stigmata (Osler/Janeway/Roth) and persistently positive S. aureus blood cultures, diagnose native-valve infective endocarditis; give broad empiric MRSA-active cover for the shock, then de-escalate to a beta-lactam once MSSA is confirmed, and involve the endocarditis/surgical team early for abscess and heart failure.
